blocks.x: Okay, let's see. Could you give your name, the first name? Wilbert Tillman. Wilbert Tillman. And let's see, where are we today? Is this Toledano Street?
2318 Toledano, apartment 1.
And today's date is January the...
20th. January 20th. January 20th. Yeah, 1966.
Yeah, New Year's rolled around. Oh, yeah. And my name is Dick Allen, and you got a name too, huh?
My name is Sabina Franco.

All right. So, let's see, what we're going to talk about. Bill Russell already talked to you once, so I just wanted to follow up on it and ask you a few questions about your relatives. I never did understand. You had a cousin or an uncle or something. What was his name? Batiste that played? Oh, yeah. Joe Batiste. Mm-hmm. He was a banjo player. What kin was he to you? Huh? He was kin to you? Yeah, that was my cousin. Your cousin, huh? Mm-hmm. And you had a lot of other cousins and in-laws and everything that played, huh?
Well, Joe Batiste played and John played and John got Sam Casme played and William Casme played. Those were John's brothers? All my first cousins, yeah. Yeah.
Well, how does Vernon Gilbert fit in there? I know he was kin to John. Is he kin to John?
Vernon Gilbert?
Yes, he's in-
He was on that number of our man. He was kin to John.
He wasn't any kin to you, huh?
No.
I just wondered. I'd heard that he was just a cousin. No, he was just a trumpet player. Yeah.
And what about your brother-in-law? Alan Gaudet? He's a trumpet player. That's his wife here now.
Oh, yeah?
That's his wife here. Oh, really?
Well, I heard Monday Night's things a lot, him being a wonderful puppet player.
That's my sister's husband.
Mm-hmm. And what is, what was his, what kin was he the Huntley Gaudet?
Yeah, that's what I mean.
Huntley? Yeah.
His name was Hunter Gaudet.
Oh, Hunter Gaudet.
Hunter Gaudet, yeah. Hunter Allen Gaudet.
Oh, I see. That's the same man.
That's the same man, yeah.
That's what I always thought, but I never did know for sure, so I thought I'd ask him. Yeah. Sure. And let's see, I guess that about takes care of most of the people in your family that played.
Well, my brother played. Oh, yeah? Yeah, that's my brother, Edward Tillman.
Let's get your name on here so we can, your name is? Edward. Mm-hmm. And what did you play?

I played trombone, trumpet, and drums. Oh, you got it right quite a bit, huh? Oh, yeah. Did you all play together much? Yeah, he played with me when I first started playing. Mm-hmm. Yeah, we made up a little band among ourself, you know? Mm-hmm.
And what were you playing then in the band? Chant ball. You were playing trombone then. I made some notes about that first band. I wanted to ask you, who are the other members in it?
Well, I had me and my brother-in-law.
You and your brother-in-law got that? That's the first band?

That was my first band. That's the band we made up. Me and my brother-in-law, my brother, and my brother's son, and Joe Baptiste, and old man Niles Ross on bass. That's where our first band was, first of all the band. Mm-hmm.
Wait a minute. I didn't get that straight. Who was on drums?
Your... Ernest Gardette Jr.
Ernest Gardette Jr., I see. Mm-hmm. Well, I got it straight now. Which was the Peerless band?
That was the band. See, we made up that band and started playing among ourselves. And then when we got where we could play enough to go out and play, we named it the Peerless Band.

And who was the manager? Huh? Who was the manager? My brother-in-law, Gaudet. Mm-hmm. He was a leader too? Leader and manager. Yeah, leader and manager. He took care of everything. I never did get down, uh, why they called you Bird. That's another thing I wanted to ask you about.
Well, I was just a nickname, uh, Filipino sailor started to call me when I was in the Navy.
Mm-hmm.

That's, uh, he could never say Wilbert, so he just said, well, I'll call you Bird. And he started to call me Bird, and from then on everybody started calling me Bird. Mm-hmm. That was a Filipino boy, originally, was young. Mm-hmm.
He was trying to say Wilbert and now he could come out with the Bird?
Yeah, well, it's...
Wasn't it you look like a Bird or anything?
Well, they said I looked like a Bird. Really? Yeah. Yeah. I had a high chest, you know.
Oh, I see. Yeah. Mm-hmm. And what all different instruments have you played? Did I play? Mm-hmm.

Well, I first started on clarinet. Mm-hmm. Then saxophones began coming out and fellas induced me to try to get a saxophone. But after I got the saxophone, I wanted to be a trumpet, which I wanted to be a trumpet, and then I started playing off-set. Mm-hmm. And then I started on trumpet, and I played trumpet in the band until the Eureka band got without a bass player. Mm-hmm. And they encouraged me to play a few of them. I said, well, I don't know nothing at all about the bass. They said, well, you play the trumpet, the bass finger just likes the trumpet. Mm-hmm. So they talked me in and finally I made up my mind to go and make the trumpet. Well, they found out I made out so well, they induced me to try to keep on trying to learn it. Mm-hmm. So I already knew how to read music. I didn't worry about that part. So I got old man, Professor Delmore, to give me one lesson. I got a bass and finger and the distance in the tone, and after that I was going to play myself. That's what caused me to play bass because trumpet really was my...
It's trumpet and saxophone and clarinet and bass.
Clarin and bass, yeah.
And that's all, huh? Mm-hmm. Didn't you have a string bass at one time and a trumpet? I have it not. Mm-hmm. I have string bass, no. You ever play any jobs on that?

No. I just thought that was learning to play. Mm-hmm. I see. How many different saxophones did you play? Well, I could play all the sax. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I mean, turning it out or I never tried a bass, but once I got it, it was all the same. It was a different mouthpiece and different tone, but the tone doesn't enjoy me because years back I used to play the soprano and it's got a free tone in all of them.
Yeah.
Yeah, I used to play soprano, play it alto, play it tenor, play it a little baritone. Any of the reasons, I didn't worry about that.
Yeah. Yeah, I guess you could play a vowel trombone if you had to, I'm sure.
Well, I know I could. I guess I'd have been out on the vowel because I had bought that for a normal test.
Mm-hmm.

You see, and this was going to take jobs like after I was playing bass on the orchestra jobs, I was going to take the vowel trombone on for a normal test, feature numbers, you know. But I took sick right behind when I just had a vowel and I didn't practice. But I'm still going to learn it. I'm going to learn it because I like it. Yeah. I never bought an instrument yet in my life that I didn't learn how to play if I kept it rhyming on.
Yeah. When did you take sick? I'm trying to remember.
I take the sick August the 26th, 1964. Mm-hmm.
And over here, aren't you? Yeah, a little over here. That's a long time, but you can get around some now when you can.

Oh, man, when I first stayed in sick, I couldn't stand up last night when I was trying to walk. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I couldn't stand up. And you came back by the house and saw me back then. Mm-hmm. I remember. Yeah, I was confined to bed, man, just lay down and get up and sit down. I couldn't stand up. But now, since I've been walking with the pressures, I do fine.
I go anywhere I want to go. Yeah, I played with the project down in charity. Mm-hmm. Yeah, Clyde Wilson, you know that English trumpet player said he'd do it at charity one night.
Yeah, I played the project down in charity.
Mm-hmm. How many jobs have you played? Since I've been sick? Yeah.
I played Preservation three times in the charity. That's a cool job. Mm-hmm.
Who do you play at in Preservation? Who do you play with down there?

With Bill and Diddy. Mm-hmm. And Kid Punch. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Mac Jeffrey was hiding there all the time with Bill and Diddy while Nelson and them was away, you know? So whenever he hired me, I'd either play down there with Punch or play with Bill and Diddy. Mm-hmm. But at the hospital, that was my project. And I hired who I want to hire. Mm-hmm. So I had a keg ladder myself and uh, After you Proyber, Andrew Martin and Lars Trottet on drums.
How many pizzas is that? Six or five? Six. Yeah. Banjo?

On his roof, yeah. On guitar or banjo? Yeah, he's on guitar. He wasn't supposed to come with the banjo, but he brought a guitar. It didn't make any difference with me as long as I had a 690, you know?
Mm-hmm. Ernie Cagnoletti, yeah. Yeah, Cagnoletti. On trumpet. Uh-huh. Yeah. Are you going to continue on with this Young Tuxedo Orchestra? You going to use that name?
Mm-hmm. I'm going to try to hold it as long as I can, Dick. Mm-hmm. I'm going to change it. I don't have no reason for changing it.
Mm-hmm.
See, I was playing with him when John died.
Mm-hmm.
And I'd take it over, but unfortunately I'd take the sick.
Mm-hmm.
I couldn't run the brass band, so I just told Morgan, I'd turn the brass band part over to him. And any job come through for the brass band, come to me, I'd contact him.
Yeah.
But the orchestra part, I'm going to handle that. Mm-hmm. I see.
So, how long has John had that orchestra?

The Young Tuxedo Orchestra? Well, I'd like to tell you. You might can remember that better than me, because when he was coming to Tyler's, we was playing with Joe Everett. It was Iber and Tillman's Dixie Land. So, after I left, I mean after Joe died, well then John made up the band and named it Young Tuxedo.
Mm-hmm.

You see, and he had the Young Tuxedo Orchestra and Young Tuxedo Brass Band, just like I did. But now here's where the catch come in. He wasn't named the Young Tuxedo before that, he was named Tulane. Mm-hmm. See, the Tulane Brass Band broke up. Mm-hmm.
We'll be turning it off. We were talking about how they had the Tulane.
Yeah, well see, after Tulane Brass Band broke up, John was taking that over.
Mm-hmm.
When it broke up, then he named his band, the Young Tuxedo. Mm-hmm. Because the Tulane Band was run by Al Light. You remember Al Light.
Yeah, I knew him.
And John said, well, he was going to go for a 7. And he named his band Young Tuxedo. Mm-hmm. See, and then he made Young Tuxedo Orchestra and Young Tuxedo Brass Band.
Well, Landry was the leader of the Tulane, huh? Uh-huh.

Landry was the leader of the Tulane. Landry was the leader of the Young, I mean, the Eureka. And then Willie Wilson was leader. Then Landry led. Then Landry, from Landry to T-Boy, they led leader. See, that's when leaders come down and then after T-Boy, then Poison. I see. Well, who managed the Young Tuxedo? John managed it himself. But he always considered whoever he hired for the Trump player, you know, was the leader. But he managed his own stuff. But didn't Rodgers get some of those jobs or someone? Ernie Rogers? Ernie Rogers? Well, he was just a drummer or just a bamboo
bamboo

bamboo ! Yeah, he was just a member. Oh I see. Because he knew a societist and knew him from playing with other bands, you know. And quite naturally after he joined with John or any work he got, he just turned it over to John and then he still went on to him.
Well how do these men in the grass band get jobs anyway, huh? Well they get them all kinds of ways.

They get them through being members of organizations. They get them through friends that know them better than they know others. See if they, it's like if you have a friend, regardless of what he is, if you got something that you can do in his way, you give it to him. Now regardless of who he hired, it don't make no difference. You're looking to him. Yeah. You're looking to the void. See, now all you want boys to do is bring you a band. You understand? And that's the way it is with them boys. See now I had a fella came down here from Gonzales the Sunday before Christmas I think I told you about that. It was down here the Sunday before Christmas. Well I turned that job over to Morgan. They had been running over in the Orleans for three weeks looking for anybody that knew who had the Young Tuxedo band in charge. People told them about Puss and they told them about Paul Barbarine, they told them about different fellas. Somebody at the Union Hall wanted to book me and said no, the members wants the Young Tuxedo in that band that we don't even listen for. Yeah. Well he went to the Union Hall and the Union Hall told them, they said well, we know Wilbert Tillman runs the Young Tuxedo, Arkin, and probably if you contact him he could tell you about the brass band. So the man came here one night from Wake and knocked on door and said are you Wilbert Tillman? I said yeah. He said well we from Gonzales. He said you all played for us three or four years ago and we've been had all kinds of bands. But the members told us if you didn't find the Young Tuxedo don't bring no band. So that's the way that comes through. See now he found me, I signed up the contract and everything with it myself. And I explained to him, I said I'm sick, I can't walk no more. I said but don't worry I'll have the Young Tuxedo band there. And I contact Andrew right away you see. Now to let the people up there know that it was Young Tuxedo band I went with them. They come and got me in the car and take them up there. See now them people didn't know nobody in the Young Tuxedo band but me and John. See I could listen, probably anybody up there that was Young Tuxedo band if they saw me. So after I told Morgan about it, Morgan said well you better come and go. Because they know you, they don't know me. So that's the way those things go you see.
What about the churches, do they ever get any jobs through churches? Who is that? You, I mean with your band. Do the churches ever hire brass bands? Well no, they never hire them.
I mean all that kind of work comes through organizations.
The organizations marches a band too at church but the church doesn't.

The only job you get from a church that like a group of people is meeting somewhere and it's not their church and they're going to march from that church to their new location then the church will hire you. But like for fumes or any other occasion they don't hire. Anything pertaining to churches they'll hire for march you know. But other than that fumes or anything else that's going on somebody else is hired.
Well now I wonder about, is it, I mean your orchestra, do they get many jobs through organizations?
Well practically all the jobs they get me through organizations. You see if it's a funeral.
No I mean the orchestra, the dance orchestra.

Oh the dance orchestra? Well they get that through organizations too. They get it through pleasure clubs. It's like this season all the balls is going on. They're hiring whatever band they want for balls. And people giving dances, public dances, they hire. Organizations giving a public dance or pleasure club or anything and they know it, they'll hire. I mean that's all the contact you have. You see the only thing that's pointless here in Northern which you know that is burdensome to the quality. If you don't get out there you don't have nothing pointless. And all the other jobs come from the outside. Anybody that know the orchestra, know someone in the orchestra, want their type of music, you hire. Some people want rock and roll, some want progressive, some want Dixieland, but it all comes through different categories. Now you take like out the country club, they don't want nothing but Dixieland there. See? So I mean that's the contact the musicians have. We don't get anything through the union in the line of jobs unless somebody particularly asks for a certain band.
Maybe a little project once in a while. Just a project, yeah.

Well I mean that's the thing. And you don't get that for about once a year. I mean they have so many members and then they be trying to help, you know, help one another out. You know one probably get all up and the other one don't get none. Now what they will do, like I'm sick, they'll give me one because that helps me. I have to keep my card and thing up. Which I get my card about a year, you see. I never have got a quarter card since I've been in it. I always get my card about a year. But like I'm sick and handicapped now, that helps me out. I don't have anything, anything coming in.
You dropped your sick off.

Anything coming in on a person down sick out. See? Because I don't have, I don't have no way of making a living. Now before I had a living because I could work and I could play music too. See, I don't have no way of doing that.
I see. Well the, what about the dance halls? You know, I'm not even. Are there any more of them going? No. Dance halls? No.

I'll try, like I say, around this season of the year. There's nothing happening, that's no dance halls. All the crap get a cuff. Every now and then that'll give something, you know. Yeah. Big four. There's a couple of spots. I mean there's nothing much to it. Doudrop, it's a night club, they have about five pieces. They got a couple of other spots with small combos in them, you know. Yeah. This is a great big dead town, that's what it is. As far as the music life, there's no music life. I see. All it's started getting the benefit of this, that's working in the spots around the Boydman Street and the Quarters. And well in True Jeffery he's been getting great smaller contacts with the bands, send them out of town. So every time he send one or two bands out for no while, that's going to hire more horn musicians, which I think is one of the best things you could ever have. I mean to have somebody interested enough to try to keep you doing a little something, you know what I mean? Now you take that Bourbon Street Club, well personally Albert men get straight smaller work out of town, but it don't be for a little time, you see, they don't stay that long. Albert who? Albert French. Oh yeah. Albert French. Yeah they might go off for one or two days and they come right back and the only time outside to get to work in there is when they're gone. The man really would like to have them in there every night. But they work four or five nights I think and they're off by two.
That's Dixieland Hall you're talking about.

Dixieland, yeah. Because Kid Howard they work some off dates but the musicians don't get a chance to work as many off dates in there as they do in Preservation. See, because Jack Fris, in most of those, since he's been playing himself, well quite naturally he's hustling on both angles. And the out of town, the out of town attraction means more to him than staying there. Because if he stay there he don't do nothing but work. So he don't worry about playing at Preservation but when he get on the road, well then he plays.
Oh yeah, I see. So he makes it both ways then. Oh yeah. And then the other people come.

He makes it both ways and they hurt me too. See, because we didn't even play the same instrument. I mean, Charles used to hire me on, he played myself. So that's kind of a hard shift for me but what I'm going to do, he's the boss.

That's right. Well I know when I first found John up about it, you know, to come to the Preservation Hall. Uh huh. But, alright, he told me some of the different places he played but I've forgotten different organizations he played for. Who were you playing most of your work for before Preservation Hall started? With the orchestra?

Well, we were just spotting around. I mean, we didn't have nothing for him. We didn't have to spotting around, catch him sometimes private forters and sometimes, you know, public dancers. It's just a occasion, nothing for him. We wasn't on nothing for him.
But who were you playing for? Who were some of the different organizations and people? Were you playing for Society People on St. Charles Avenue or?

Well, we played for some of them too. We got one up there I think on Robinson's show or St. Charles, we used to pray for them. Well, we'd always have them when they, like when you're, I think it was a two-led bunch lived in there.
Might have been.
Yeah, and uh. Yeah, I think it's a fraternity.
Yeah, it's a fraternity. Yeah, it's a fraternity. Yeah, it's a fraternity job.

Yeah, we played that, uh, got one up there on, uh, Maple and, uh, Pine. Yeah, Maple. Maple and Pine, or Bute and Pine. And we played, oh, a bunch of them there on Audubon Street. Right there by the Newcomb College. In that block between Ferret and Zepo. Mm-hmm. When we played practice, I'd say, in that block there. I mean, when they would hide something.

Did you play mostly for white or mostly for color? Oh, mostly for white. Mostly for white. Mostly for white. Mostly for white, yeah. Okay. Well, if you played a parade all day, would they hire you at night to play the dance with some of these societies? Sure. Sure. Same band, huh? Sure. It must have been hard on you after you walk all day. Oh.
The Jolly Bunch is about the oldest one we got here. Yeah. And we didn't play at that one. We didn't play at dance that night. Yeah.
How long's the Jolly Bunch last? Let's see, it starts at what?
It starts at 10 o'clock tomorrow, lasts at six.
Yeah, well, that's long enough. I thought, hey, what's that going on?
Well, the carnival starts at seven. Yeah. We played for the Jefferson City Busters and the Lions.
Mm-hmm.

Oh, I played for them from way back in gone years time. And I had to leave home at five o'clock in the morning. And then the time when we first was playing for the old Eleanor's, I don't want to miss Eleanor's with the guys, now it's a bunch of kids. We used to leave home at five to start at six. And for about seven o'clock in the morning, man, we'd be there at about fifteen stops. Just coming out of one stop and going to another. Yeah. And then we had to go to Cornell Street and come back up and didn't get off until six o'clock in the evening. Sixty-six we used to play. And at that time, it wasn't getting but ten dollars.
Yeah. Did you play with Garnier's band? Yeah. Were you a regular member?
Yeah, I was a regular member. And then Garnier was my director in the WPA band. Oh, I see.
I didn't know that.
Yeah, Garnier was director in the WPA band.
Was he the main director? He was the main director at that time.
At one time.
Yeah, I didn't know that.
He was the main director. They had him and Lewis the man after him, which I got Lewis there. And we had Pinch back T-Roll. You remember Pinch?
I never met him. I never met Lewis the man, neither. Yeah, I was.

I'm the one who got Lewis the man in the WPA band. In fact, I was the first trumpet player in the WPA band, could play anything that people could understand. There was a bunch of them in there. But Gilbert had the band then. Gilbert had the band way before Martina came. And what Gilbert did, he got in there and he'd taken everybody who said he was a musician. Then he classified him. He classified him just like a school, like it started from first grade on up. And he rated him according to their plan abilities.
Which Gilbert is that?
I don't know if the last name was Gilbert. I can't think of it.
What did he play?
Nothing. He was just a director of the WPA band.
Oh I see.

Yeah. Well he classified the men which he would benefit the musicians more than anybody they had there if they'd let him see it there. But they felt like he wasn't doing it the way they wanted and they got rid of Gilbert and they got old man Martina. And that broke up all his ideas was. His ideas was to get so many men together that couldn't play that much and let somebody go over and teach them and rate them on like that. And the men that was qualified could read pretty good, you know, it would be a band up with them. Which it was a better building ability for musicians than it was when Martina came. When Martina took it over, instead of him building it up he tore it up. See because everybody couldn't play he put them out of the band.
So he didn't give him a chance to learn.
He didn't give him a chance to learn. That broke it down you see. That's a shame. Back to Garnier. Who was in Garnier's band usually?
Who was in the brass band? Well I can't think of the man's band. The only man I can think of was in Garnier's brass band at that time was me and

him. He was in the brass band. He was in the brass band. He was in the brass band. Yeah, that was way back. Yeah, I couldn't think of it. What were you playing then? I played clarinet then. And what did the...
Knox was playing bass then.
What did the... Oh, which clarinet did you play?
B flat or E flat? E flat.
You ever play E flat?
No. Never.
What did Garnier play? Garnier was trumpet player.

Is that the Jalma Garnier? Yeah. That's who I thought you were talking about. Yeah. That's who I thought you were talking about. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He's the only one I know around here. He might have some. I know Booker T played with him for a while. I don't know.
Yeah. But he was probably playing bass drums. And Didi played with him for a while, I know. Yeah.
Well, Didi played with Garnier and Didi played with John too. Oh yeah. Yeah. He used to be a member of the Tuxley band. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Yeah. That's right. Yeah.
Yeah. That's right. Yeah.
Yeah. That's right.
Oh, let's see.
Man, there's so much I want to ask you about. There's so many different people. Just keep on asking. Yeah. Let the money grow up.
Yeah. Don't let your pocket get no hole in it.

Yeah, well, we can do it again. Anyway, what about the Creole Serenaders? Creole Serenaders? Did you ever play with them? Peter Boccage had them. Oh no, I never. You never played with them. I just wanted a few.
The only playing I did with Pete was, you know, since these recent years. Yeah, I played on the job, but I never was a member of his band. I see.
Oh, we were talking about the Tulane band and we never did get down who was in that band, who the different members were.
Well, I can't tell you all of them either, but I can tell you some of them. Yeah, sure. Ernest Rogers was one I know, and Big Al Landry, and Happy Remus, that's Bill Matthews' brother.
Which drum did he play?
He played saxophone. He played snare?
Uh-huh. And Ernest Rogers played what? Ernest Rogers was snare drum player too, but they played in that same band but at different
times. At different times, yeah. Yeah, see. Rogers was with them when they originally set up that Tulane band. And after Rogers then they're taking on Happy. Mm-hmm.
Okay, I think it's just about, uh, to run out with him.

Okay, let's see, this is reel two of Wilbert Tillman, January 20th, 1966. We were talking about the Tulane Van, and you say you can't remember too many more other than those we just named, huh? No, I can't remember them. That's too far back. Oh, yeah. Well, did you ever play with the original Toxia? The original Toxia? Yeah, when...
I never was a member, but I had played with them during Papa Celestan time. Yeah, I played with them, but I never was a member of them.
I see. Do you remember who was in that band, any of the people on that you heard?
Yeah, John Porter, Lewis Tillman, Celestan, and...
Excuse me, we better check and see what instruments they played, because some of them played two or three, you know? John Porter played...
Well, John Porter played bass and baritone. All right. In the same band, different times?
Yeah. Oh, I see.

You see, sometimes they'd use him on baritone, sometimes they'd use him on bass. I see. And Louis DeMere was a trumpet player, and Celestan was a trumpet player. And they used to use lavender occasion, used to use Peter Bocard. I think Peter Bocard was once a member. Mm-hmm. He was a regular member of the band. And they had Sonny Henry on trombone. I can't play swells with Pam Trombone on the side.
Did you know Louis Armstrong down here?

Me and Louis Armstrong was in the homes at the same time when he was learning. Oh, yeah? Yeah, I tried to get in the band and there had to be an instrument cleaner first. Mm-hmm. And I used to clean Louis and them horns to try to work my way up to the band.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, that was the best band the homes ever had.
Well, they had some good people in it, I know from what I hear. Oh, yeah.

And there was shots, shots was in there with shots and little George Washington was on trombone. Jerry was on, I called Jerry to call him. He was on trumpet. And well, drums and them other instruments. Kid ran in. Huh? Yeah, really, they'd come up all under us. Kid ran in. Was he in the home? Yeah, we was all in the homes and all the same band. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I was the instrument cleaner. I wasn't playing nothing, man.
What about Joe Rene? Was he in there? Who was that? Joe Rene. Kid ran in.

No, he wasn't in there. Joe Rene, Joe Rene come up to be a drummer way after Rene started playing out, you know? Mm-hmm. And then he played clarinet, learned clarinet, you know? But that was weird. Ran in there, been in the homes, learned how to play and come out and play it around a good while before him and Joe got together. Mm-hmm.
I see. So there must have been a pretty good band. How big a band was it? At that time?
Yeah, in the homes. They had about, uh, well, when they would take them on the street, they'd take about twelve. He must have had about twenty-piece bands. Mm-hmm.
But they wouldn't use them all, huh?
No, when they'd go on the street, they would take out a ten or twelve-piece band. Mm-hmm. The boys that could really play, you know? Mm-hmm.
Did they read much? Do you know if they were reading them?

Well, I'll tell you, they learned them both ways. I guess that's why so many of them is able to play like that today. Now, Professor did. Mm-hmm. He would strictly try to learn them the music. Mm-hmm. But he wouldn't stop them from playing by air if they had that gift of talent. Mm-hmm. And that's why they grew so fast to be musicians. Mm-hmm. See, now, Lewis played a long time by air until he began, you know, to see the light to read.
Mm-hmm. Let's see. That's interesting. Uh, did you play with the, uh, Onward Brass Band ever? The old Onward? Yeah, the old Onward. No. What about the Excelsior?
I didn't play with any of them. Uh, Old Man Allen? What about him? Oh, you know I played with him. Yeah. He had one of my first bands.
Tanner Island. Mm-hmm. What was your first brass band job? Do you remember?

Uh, I knew it was, the first brass band job I had was with Old Man Allen and that was in Algeist. Mm-hmm. How old were you then? Uh, I was, um, twenty, let me see, it must have been around twenty-three, twenty-four years ago.
You've been out of the Navy a while when you got there.
I came out of the Navy in 1919. I didn't start to playin', really out playing music till 1922.
Mm-hmm.
I see.
All right. What about Allen's band? Who was in that? Uh. You don't remember? No, I had, I know me and Gordette was playing with him.

Mm-hmm. Used to hire us from this side of the river. And, uh, Happy Remus and John Casney and his son, Red Island. That's all I can think of. He's been playin' trumpet all his life. Oh. Yeah, he never played in Red Island. Yeah. Uh, one thing I never did get straight, uh, what about this, uh, young tuxedo? When- when- when was the young tuxedo brass band found at what age?
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . When was the Young Tuxedo? When was the Young Tuxedo Brass Band founded? What age? Was that after Landry died or before he died?
That was before he died because he played with Jones for a while. Yeah, that was before he died.
But the Tulane had kind of broken up.
Tulane had broke up, yeah. It wasn't the more Tulane.
Was it before World War II?
Oh yeah, I think we had before World War II. Yeah, I think we had that band before World War II. Yeah, I see.
Where were you playing, by the way, when the Depression came? When the Depression hit in 1929?
Around 1929. Let's see. Orchestra or Brass Band?
Both of them. You want to turn it down? We can do it.
Yeah, turn it out. That's what I think that thing was hot to me. Yeah. That's my youngest sister, Dick. I think he might have to work, doesn't he?
Yeah, I believe so. Just pull that plug. We were talking about the Young Tuxedo and Depression. Which orchestra were you playing with when the Depression hit?

Well, in the Depression, me and Joe, we were in an orchestra. We had, you know, our little outfits. And then, like all musicians, just playing with anybody high, you know. You had everything you could. And the Brass Band? Brass Band was the same way. I worked with all the brass bands in the city that they had.
Yeah, this is around 1929 and 30. Yeah, I worked with all of them. Well, when you were playing music, when you first started, there were speakeasers and stuff there? Oh yeah.

What were they like? Well, they were just like, these people call them nightclubs now, but they were speakeasers then. The ballroom, they either played right in the ballroom or they had like a room in the back. Oh, turn it out.
All right, now, let's see. We're talking about how they ran the speakeasers. Is it just like a regular ballroom?

Yeah, you see, it was a drawing proposition and a moment of making propositions for the ballrooms. In other words, they'd hire a little four-piece band in there on a Saturday night, a Friday night, a Sunday night. Well, that held a crowd. That's why they started to call them speakeasers, you see. And the band would play so many pieces and then they would stop and the people would be constantly drinking all throughout the night. Instead of calling them nightclubs, they'd call them speakeasers. Did they ever get raided? Would they hear the band come in? Oh, no, they'd write permission for them, you know, to operate. Just like now you've got to have a- Of course, they did it lately enforce that law about this music tax and all that. But they was all right with the law. I mean, as far as the law part was concerned, it was taken care of. And they had their license to operate and so many nights they allowed them a week to operate with music, you know, and on nights that they wasn't. They had music on nights they wasn't allowed well then they'd read it. But sometimes they'd get caught in the read and they'd have everything, but it wouldn't be on the column of the police. It would be like somebody went out, snatched somebody's pocketbook or something. Or held up somebody and run up in places for a hideout while they'd find who they wanted. They'd come pull an old joint. Mm-hm. the wind and paid and went up. Police would come up and they paid to go to jail. If I'd have stayed on the bank. So it was just one of them things. But it was 100% better then than it is now because if they were still outspeakeasers, musicians would have weight. See that's the thing with concerts. Anything that hurt a musician don't help him. Now you see when jukeboxes first come out, all the people who was hiring their little band, they cut them off, they had to put a jukebox in there. You go in there and you drop a nickel on whatever record you want in. Well they didn't need the musicians. Sometimes they'd hire a band. And before the people would come and ask you could you play the piece, they'd go put a nickel on the jukebox. The man said if they were ready to jukebox, they were hiring no band.
When was this that the jukeboxes started to come out? Oh, I don't know.

19... Oh, around 1917 or 18, somewhere back then. When they began getting popular, you know. Just one or two places had them, but there's a group. Getting all kinds of prisms and different styles and enticing more people to... I think about around 16 or 17, when they got popular.
Before you were in the Navy even, huh? Not to get them here. Excuse me. Sure.
Let's see. Before they were in the... Oh yeah, yeah, it is not to get popular in the Navy. I see.
And did they get more popular as the years went on? Or you said they had more... They still have been popular. And they're getting more and more popular...

Yeah, they're still a bit more and more popular. Because they're making smaller records, they're putting out more records, the boxes is larger, they're playing hymns and songs or whatnot, progressives, they've got everything on one box now. You can go and play and get anything you want now, you see, Dixieland, Progressives. So it means it's a, if the years grow by, the improvements is growing on.
It's a miracle musicians make it at all, I swear, with everything against them.

Well that's what I'm saying, everything is a, you see now, here I die there, Dixieland. All right, just like you sitting down right now, you ask me for information, history of my life. All right, I get that. Maybe I won't never read a book with any, but the generation coming behind will read it, you understand? They don't know me, the people of the day know me. All right. That book may sell for a thousand years. I give the information for five hours an hour. The book is sold maybe five hours a book. See, that's just the way it is with the records. I mean, the musicians, a Christian group come there and we want you to cut a record, cut a tape. They cut it. All right. They make a hundred dollars, a hundred and fifty dollars. That's paid off. They don't got no more worry with that. Now if they send a hundred million records from that day, all they can do is listen at
it. Yeah, that's right.
See, that's the point of the thing.
So the people who make the money are the ones who put the records out, the publisher of the record of the book.

The public's going to make nothing. The public's going to make nothing. The only thing the leader of the band gets if he understands about, after a certain amount of records is sold, he's supposed to receive the royalty, so much percent. Other than that, what do he get? He get a leader's pay, whatever they charge to cut the tape. The members get a side man's pay.
And that's all. They don't get any.
That's all. They don't get another penny. I mean, that's all of it.
I know John used to get a few dollars.

Oh, that wasn't enough for the bar staff to put on a letter. My Me Good, the highest My Me Got was around $3.36. Is that all? That's right. Hmm. You're getting a check for $3.36 and $3.30 and $3.40, that ain't no kind of royalty to get off no record. Like that, that record is still selling yet. Yeah. And I'm the one should have been drawing the royalty on that because I'm the one made up the piece, but I didn't, instead of me saying Tillman Boogie, I told him this artist called it Everest Boogie.
Oh, that Joe Everest piece you made that up? That was my number.

We made that number up during the other time. We was playing a few of them called them. And I made, that's the first time I made that hoop on the base. And Joe looked at me and said, you got something new? He said, well you learned that. I said, that's all right. He said, well what you don't name that? I said, I'm going to name it after you. I'm going to call it Everest Boogie. But it should have been named Tillman Boogie because then nobody knows nothing about it. And they had a bass player in the whole city of New York and can play it like me right now. None of them didn't all try. Joshua didn't try. Because I don't know what I'm going to make on it myself until I make it.
Your style just comes to you. That's right.

That's right. I make whatever comes in my mind to make it and ain't nobody else going to ever be a player. See, because when I find out they're playing the way they think they got it, I'll play it and put something else in.
Yeah, well I never have heard anybody else ever do that. They ain't going to never do it. No, I mean I've heard them try to copy and all that. That's right. They can't cut.

They tried to copy. I don't know. I went down to Jaffer's couple times and he asked me to play it. I play it and he get his horn and play along with me and I just take down. I say good lick. It's all right. She makes the hoop. They don't make it. Brown tried to make it. Minor tried to make it. I don't worry about them. I make it. Make it when I get ready and put anything in it I want. It's like Larry come there one night. Larry said, I never heard a man make a triple turn on the best way to do. And he brought some white boy there with him and the white boy said, I never could triple turn. Larry said, play it again. Make it again. I know I don't be dumb. I know he's trying to catch on. You might make something sound like it. But you can't make what the other man made. You can't do it to see if you're like them boys write copies of Louis Armstrong and style, copies of Al Hoyt style. But when they play it, if they don't have a style of their own, they ain't play nothing right at all. You got to have your own style of music. If everybody played the same way, music wouldn't be worth two cents to listen to it. No. No. No, it wouldn't be any good at all. No, no it wouldn't be any good at all.
When you were coming up then you didn't listen to anybody much? Oh yeah.
Man I don't know, I just looked like it was with me for the learner to play music. When I was coming up I used to have them little ten flutes, I don't know if you ever remember
them.

But I was one of the best flute players they had in college. And that made me believe I wanted to be a clarinet because I could play so much of the flute. And at that time we had the band Wagons. This furniture wagon used to move with the furniture around the city, the trucks used to move them on the wagon. And on Sunday they put a band on the wagon for different clubs and the clubs would ride in tally holes. I don't know if you ever saw a tally hole. Now what is it? A tally hole is made, it's long, long this way with a seat on each side. Just like the old electric cars used to be made. A tally hole is made like that with a step on the back for her to get up in. And either two horses or one horse. That's what the clubs used to ride in. And the band would be on the furniture wagon. You didn't see no bands on no trucks advertising it. All this car decorating. They used to decorate tally holes. Fowler Perez and tally holes. I caught them many witness for running around, filing behind bands on trucks that play at every corner, you know, for dancing and picnics and lawn parters, getting lawn parters in them tally.
Well the club would be advertising their dance on the tally hole? Yeah.

And all that tally hole. You didn't see much that walking like you do now advertising. They'd get them as big as the club was, they'd get them in the tally holes and decorate them up with all kinds of pretty paper, ribbon and things like that. Get a band stop on the corner and go to the plane and draw traction to the people and then they'd get out there and dance and clown. I mean that was in them days. Yeah, that must have been something to see then. Yeah, y'all think y'all seen something now, but I mean in them olden times it was something for real history. Something worthwhile. Now them little tourist buggers what they, what they used in the quarters now, they used to use some of them. In fact, two or three members, you know, get one of them and use it. Most of the whole club would be in tally hole.
I wouldn't have given anything to see that.

Yeah, well everything got so modern and all those undertaker paws and things that used to have, then they all did away with them. Liberty stables, they went out, sent all the horses and mules and things back on the country. See in the time I'm talking about was when they didn't have all this fancy carnival floor parade. That's what made the older people say carnival look so dead to them because they used to use the wagon floors. They didn't have all this jeep pulling by so fast. They had horses, mules pulling them floats and the parade was slower and more prettier and you could see more of it. But now if the parade goes by so fast you can't realize it's a parade. You can't get a chance to see what it really is.
Yeah, they're no good. They take long enough to get there but they go by just like that.
Well yeah, they get there all right. If it take them a day, I mean you still would see more of it. Yeah. Yeah.
Have you played out of town much? Different places?

Through my career? Yeah. Yeah, I was playing on the, on the Washer Tar, running from foot of Canal Street to Camden, Arkansas. I played on that boat. It was a freight and excursion boat you know. I played on that around five or six years with Sun White. And then I did quite a bit of traveling all through the state of Mississippi with Foster Lewis jazz band. I did a little traveling with my own band, but I'm talking about bands that I played with you know, in constant. We used to go all over and bugger loose and crazy like that. I wasn't making no northern trips. But we was covering states such as Mississippi and Louisiana. You did go to Washington once.
Well I went to Washington to do Dixieland. Yeah. Yeah, I played in Washington.

What about, was it different playing in these different little towns around? Was there any difference in the music? I don't know. Same thing. They didn't want more of one type or another, huh? Dixieland. That's what they wanted.

Same thing. Yeah, they wanted Dixieland. Yeah. No soft music, right? Well the only time it would require soft music would be like playing in a private home. But if you were to play in a house, you'd be playing in a house, you'd be playing in a house. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. unless it's in a place like that, what do you call that out there where Nunez to play in the quarters? Where then people eat at?
Gee, I don't know. He played so many different places.
Well, there's one of these places they advertise on the air all the time, tell you how much a meal is in the...
Quarter to sisters?
Might be, but this place here uses about three pieces nightly. It has a piano and a guitar and something else, but it's all soft. It's all soft music, right?
Brennan's? Brennan's, yeah. Yeah, Brennan's. He played that.

Well, you see a place like that, it requires soft music for a simple reason. There's no dancing, and people is talking, and they mostly want the music for entertainment. And if they would use brass in there, it would drown the people's voice. They'd be sitting right at the table and they couldn't hear and understand what they was talking about. So those are kind of places that always did and always will require soft music. But any hall, night club, country club, or any of them kind of places, they want real authentic Dixieland music. Out loud, never come tell you too loud unless you got your mic sitting where it's picking up too loud. They might tell you to cut it down. But other than that, it's all the same thing.
What about quadrilles? Were they playing any quadrilles when you started?

Not when I started. Well, yeah, they were playing, but I mean I wasn't. They were still dancing, quadrilles, shatters, and walls. But I never played quadrilles. During my time, coming along, the quadrilles was going out. And now and then somebody will hire a band and ask them, can they play a quadrilles? Well, if they never played it, they can't play it. And Peter Bocards is the honest man around here that I know now that might have a couple of sets of quadrilles that he could rent to a band, you know, or play with a band or something like that. But you know, now Percy, Percy might have some because his daddy had all types of really couldn't be in a teacher. He might have some, but I can tell you, I teach younger musicians about a quadrilles that look at you like you ain't got good things. You don't see no more shadows and you don't see no more walls. People don't dance together now. The boys be jumping on one side, the floor and the girls be jumping on the other side. I don't know when they ever get together to call it a dance. Beats me. I don't know when they get
together at all. Where they stand apart. I'm telling you, it's really rough. Did you ever see a skating

shoddish? Well, we used to have them long years ago, but I never did see them. We had them here though. What is it anyhow? I just heard about them. Well, now there's two kinds. There's a kind you can dance in a hole and there's a car and you dance on ice, with ice skis. But the most of them, the kind that you're talking about is the kind that they used to dance in a hole. But they used to have them long years ago. And I was small. They used to have a skating shoddish back at Lincoln Park. Old Lincoln Park. But I was too small. I couldn't remember that. Never did see it. And a lot of people wouldn't have let me went nowhere,
because they were too strict on the outside at the time. Did you ever go to Lincoln Park at all later on?
Mm-mm. When I got big enough to go to Lincoln Park, it didn't want out. I used to stand in my yard and see them
when they sent that old gas balloon up on the outside. I never did find out much about that balloon. What did they do?

Well, now you see, I can tell you what they did. All I know, it went up every Sunday. We used to look at it after it got up in the air. I don't know. I don't know what the idea of setting it up. I don't know. I know positive. I don't think no people went up in it, because it was sent up by gas. And it would stay up for a little time and come down. To my idea, it was more of attraction of the park. You see? Draw people out to the park. That's what I think it was. That's the only thing I could picture it to be. It wasn't nothing that they was making no money off, because they couldn't have made nothing off it when they went there,

they stayed in there too long. I see. Oh, back to Washington. Eureka was quite a success up there. What about those other bands up there? Did you hear Chris ball about it? Oh, yeah. Chris played on the set.

Well, in fact we all played on the same concert. But they had us on different times and different hours, and then they scheduled some concerts in the day for Chris that we wasn't on, and they scheduled some for Lionel Hamilton that we wasn't on.
Seems to me we went to hear Chris together one day, when you weren't working. Yeah. That's right.

Yeah. That's right. What do you think about his band? I think he's got a wonderful band, and his wife is probably one of the best entertainers I ever heard. I mean, that girl is really an entertainer.
Do you think any of the American bands, youngsters, compared with that band?

Not my idea. For that style I'm talking about. Uh-uh. Not my idea. I heard, I'll tell you, I heard that band we went out to the airport and met that year from England. They won that Coca-Cola award. It was a German band. A German band. They had a nice band and everything, but no comparing to Chris. No comparing.
They all play modern now. Huh? They all play modern now. Oh yeah? They all change world. Those Germans don't know anything, do they? I don't know about that. Well I'm going to tell you they did.
She's going to hit me in a minute. She's German.
Yeah, she's German.

Well I wouldn't say they didn't have a good band, whatever they was, but I mean there's no comparison to Chris. Not at the time they came here, ain't I? Now that boy was playing trombone. He could sit in anybody's band. He's a wonderful trombone man. And I don't know if it was the clarinet or the trumpet player. They was good. But some of those boys I imagine they'd like anybody else when they first had the stage fright. You know what I mean? They might could produce more, but it's too stage fright to produce it.
Well that was supposed to be an amateur contest, you know? Oh it was an amateur contest. Yeah, and they were supposed to be the best amateur band.
Yeah, well that trombone player, he got inside Jim Robinson and played. I'm telling you, he wasn't nothing stopping him.
And let's see, Chris Balba played with you all in Washington. That's right, when we first got there, remember? Yeah. Or when they first got there, at the Coliseum, I think they came up.
I believe they did play. We found them there, didn't we?
Yeah, they came up and started playing with the band, remember? Yeah, that's right. In front of the Coliseum. That was something. They sounded good with the band, too.
Yeah, you see Lionel, Lionel worked his band and then he switched off and worked with that ballerina out of the picture, you see? That was their double. Yeah.
We're running out of tape. We're running out of tape. Yeah.
Okay.

This is the third reel of Wilbur Tillman, January 20th, 1966. We were talking about Washington. You said Hampton was doubling up with some... playing with his band and then some dances or something like that. Ballerina. Yeah, that's right. I remember that too.
Okay, let's see. This is the fourth reel we've done. We're talking to Wilbert Tillman. It's January 20, 1966. And your sister's here now. Could we get your name? My dear

segments.title: Opening: names, address and date of the 1966 interview
segments.summary: Tillman and Dick Allen identify themselves, the address and date, January 20, 1966; Sabina Franco gives her name.

segments.title: Tillman's musician cousins and in-laws, Batiste, Casmes, Gaudet
segments.summary: Allen follows up on Bill Russell's earlier interview: Joe Batiste, the Casme brothers and Hunter Allen Gaudet, Tillman's sister's husband; Vernon Gilbert is not kin.

segments.title: Tillman's first band, the Peerless Band, with his brother
segments.summary: His brother Edward and the family made up a little band, later named the Peerless Band, with brother-in-law Gaudet as leader and manager.

segments.title: Why he is called Bird: a Filipino sailor in the Navy
segments.summary: A Filipino sailor in the Navy could not say Wilbert and called him Bird; his high chest fit.

segments.title: The instruments he plays: clarinet, saxophone, trumpet, bass
segments.summary: He started on clarinet, moved through saxophones and trumpet, and became a bass player for the Eureka band after one lesson from Professor Delmore.

segments.title: His illness since August 1964 and recovery
segments.summary: He fell sick on August 26, 1964, was bedridden and unable to stand, and now walks with crutches.

segments.title: Playing Preservation Hall and the Charity Hospital job since falling ill
segments.summary: He has played Preservation Hall three times and led his own hospital job, listing the men he hired.

segments.title: Keeping the Young Tuxedo Orchestra after John's death
segments.summary: He intends to keep the Young Tuxedo name, handles the orchestra, and turns the brass band side over to Morgan since his illness.

segments.title: How the Young Tuxedo grew out of the Tulane Brass Band
segments.summary: John Casnet's Young Tuxedo took over after the Tulane Brass Band broke up; leaders of the Eureka and Tulane are listed and John managed his own bands.

segments.title: How brass bands get their jobs: organizations and friends
segments.summary: Brass band jobs come through organizations and personal contacts; Tillman tells how a Gonzales group tracked him down for the Young Tuxedo, and churches only hire for marches.

segments.title: How the dance orchestra gets work; the union and being sick
segments.summary: Orchestra jobs come through pleasure clubs and balls rather than the union; the union gives sick members an occasional job.

segments.title: Dance halls gone: New Orleans music scene and Preservation Hall bookings
segments.summary: Few dance halls remain; Tillman describes the thin scene, Bourbon Street clubs, and band leaders who tour out of town.

segments.title: Jobs before Preservation Hall: society and fraternity dances
segments.summary: The orchestra played private and public dances, mostly for white audiences, including fraternity houses uptown.

segments.title: Carnival parades and the Jolly Bunch
segments.summary: Playing carnival parades all day for ten dollars, and parades for the Jolly Bunch, Jefferson City Buzzards and Lions.

segments.title: Playing in Garnier's band and the WPA band
segments.summary: Garnier was a regular member and director of the WPA band; Tillman got Louis Dumaine into it as first trumpet.

segments.title: The WPA band directors, Gilbert and Martina
segments.summary: Gilbert classified the musicians by ability and built the band up; Martina replaced him and put out those who could not play.

segments.title: Who played in Garnier's brass band
segments.summary: Tillman played clarinet in Garnier's brass band, and Garnier was a trumpet player; Booker T and Didi also played with him.

segments.chapter: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
segments.title: Creole Serenaders and Peter Bocage
segments.summary: Tillman never belonged to Peter Bocage's Creole Serenaders, only playing jobs with him in recent years.

segments.chapter: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
segments.title: Members of the Tulane band
segments.summary: Ernest Rogers, Big Al Landry and Happy Remus played in the Tulane band at different times.

segments.chapter: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
segments.title: Players in the original Tuxedo band under Celestin
segments.summary: He sat in during Papa Celestin's time and lists John Porter, Louis Dumaine, Celestin, Peter Bocage and Sonny Henry.

segments.chapter: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
segments.title: Instrument cleaner in the Waifs' Home band with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He was the instrument cleaner in the Home when Armstrong learned there; he names the members and Professor's teaching methods.

segments.chapter: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
segments.title: First brass band job with Old Man Allen and his Navy years
segments.summary: His first brass band job was with Old Man Allen; he left the Navy in 1919 and began playing in 1922.

segments.chapter: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
segments.title: When the Young Tuxedo Brass Band began
segments.summary: Tillman recalls the Allen band members and says the Young Tuxedo was formed before Landry died and before World War II.

segments.title: Playing during the Depression of 1929-30
segments.summary: He worked in a small orchestra with Joe and with all the city's brass bands.

segments.title: Speakeasies and how they operated
segments.summary: Speakeasies were licensed ballrooms with small bands, and musicians fared better than now.

segments.title: Jukeboxes replace live bands
segments.summary: Jukeboxes cost musicians jobs and keep getting more popular.

segments.title: Records, royalties and who gets paid
segments.summary: Musicians get a one-time session fee while publishers profit; the leader gets leader's pay, the side men get scale.

segments.title: Everest Boogie: his bass line credited to Joe Avery
segments.summary: His bass figure became Everest Boogie, named for Joe Avery; he earned only a few dollars and believes it should be Tillman Boogie.

segments.chapter: Style and old New Orleans customs
segments.title: Having his own bass style that others cannot copy
segments.summary: Players try to copy his bass playing and fail; he insists every musician needs a style of his own.

segments.chapter: Style and old New Orleans customs
segments.title: Flute, band wagons and tally-hos advertising club dances
segments.summary: Tillman was a good flute player; furniture wagons carried bands for clubs riding in decorated tally-hos, and slower carnival floats were prettier.

segments.title: Traveling: the Washer Tar excursion boat and Mississippi tours
segments.summary: He played on a freight and excursion boat to Camden, Arkansas, with Sun White, and toured Mississippi with Foster Lewis's band.

segments.chapter: Style and old New Orleans customs
segments.title: Soft music versus Dixieland for different venues
segments.summary: Audiences everywhere wanted Dixieland; only restaurants like Brennan's need soft music.

segments.chapter: Style and old New Orleans customs
segments.title: Quadrilles and who still has the music
segments.summary: Quadrilles were going out by the time he began; he never played them, and Peter Bocage might have sets.

segments.chapter: Style and old New Orleans customs
segments.title: Lincoln Park, the skating rink and the gas balloon
segments.summary: He recalls the old Lincoln Park skating rink and the Sunday gas balloon, which he thinks drew people to the park.

segments.title: Chris Barber's band at the Washington festival
segments.summary: Tillman played the same Washington concert as Chris Barber and Lionel Hampton and praises Barber's band.

segments.title: The German amateur band and Chris's trombonist
segments.summary: He compares a German band that won an amateur award with Barber's band and praises the trombone player.

segments.title: Barber and Hampton in Washington, end of reel two
segments.summary: Chris Barber played with them at the Coliseum, and Hampton doubled his band with a ballerina act.

segments.title: Reel three and four openings
segments.summary: Allen announces the third and fourth reels on January 20, 1966, with Tillman's sister present; the audio is garbled.
